fetched_contents.text: Inflammatory Cytokines and Alzheimer’s Disease: A Review from the Perspective of Genetic Polymorphisms Abstract Neuroinflammatory processes are a central feature of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) in which microglia are over-activated, resulting in the increased production of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Moreover, deficiencies in the anti-inflammatory system may also contribute to neuroinflammation. Recently, advanced methods for the analysis of genetic polymorphisms have further supported the relationship between neuroinflammatory factors and AD risk because a series of polymorphisms in inflammation-related genes have been shown to be associated with AD. In this review, we summarize the polymorphisms of both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines related to AD, primarily interleukin-1 (IL-1), IL-6, tumor necrosis factor alpha, IL-4, IL-10, and transforming growth factor beta, as well as their functional activity in AD pathology. Exploration of the relationship between inflammatory cytokine polymorphisms and AD risk may facilitate our understanding of AD pathogenesis and contribute to improved treatment strategies. Keywords: Alzheimer’s disease, Neuroinflammation, Cytokine, Genetic polymorphism Introduction Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a common neurodegenerative disease characterized by progressive declines in cognitive and functional abilities. Amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) are its main pathological hallmarks. Aβ aggregates seem to initiate the pathogenesis of AD, while NFTs may be more involved in its progression [1]. However, the exact mechanisms by which AD occurs and develops remain ill-defined, and effective methods to cure the disease or halt the associated cognitive decline remain undiscovered. Nevertheless, neuroinflammation and oxidative stress have received increasing attention as accumulating evidence suggests their involvement in its development [2, 3]. Activation of microglia, the brain-specific macrophages, has been reported in both AD patients and animal models [4], accompanied by an activated complement system [5] and increased levels of chemokines and cytokines [6, 7]. In addition, the protective effects of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs against AD risk [8] further support the neuroinflammation hypothesis of AD. Moreover, AD is a multifactorial disease with a hereditary component, and advanced technologies for the analysis of genetic polymorphisms have identified numerous genetic loci that affect AD. Recent genome-wide association studies (GWASs) strongly support the interaction of inflammation and AD because several inflammation-related genes, such as CR1 (complement receptor 1), MS4A (membrane-spanning 4-domains subfamily A), TREM2 (triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2), and CD33 [9], have been identified as AD risk modifiers in Caucasians. The association has been further supported in other populations. For instance, variants of immune-related genes, including complement factor H [10], MS4A [11], CR1 [12], and CD33 [13] are associated with AD susceptibility in Han Chinese. Moreover, based on the findings that the levels of cytokines are altered in AD patients and that cytokines are key components of neuroinflammation, numerous case-control studies have explored the association between AD risk and genetic polymorphisms of inflammatory cytokines, primarily interleukin-1 (IL-1), IL-4, IL-6, IL-10, tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα), and transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ). However, the results have been inconsistent. Thus, a series of meta-analyses was conducted, and conclusions with high reliability were obtained. However, because genetic polymorphism analyses are increasingly used in different populations, the data in this field are continually updated. Accordingly, in the current review, we comprehensively summarize the key genetic polymorphisms of inflammatory cytokines associated with AD, including the latest evidence (summarized in Table 1). In addition, progress in the exploration of the functional activity of these polymorphisms and the mechanisms by which they modify AD susceptibility are illustrated. Table 1. fetched_contents.text: Association Between Porphyromonas gingivalis and Alzheimer’s Disease: A Comprehensive Review Abstract Background Periodontitis has long been linked to various inflammatory, chronic, and immunological diseases, such as heart disease or diabetes. Recently, there has been increasing scientific interest in the bidirectional relationship that may exist between periodontitis and the presence and progression of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), where it is hypothesized that the infiltration of oral microorganisms (mainly Porphyromonas gingivalis) into the bloodstream, which subsequently reaches the brain, causes inflammatory and neurodegenerative processes related to AD. Purpose The purpose of this review is to determine the association between Porphyromonas gingivalis and Alzheimer’s disease in older adults. Patients and Methods It was carried out using different databases such as PubMed, Web of Science, among others, of no more than 10 years old focused on older adult patients who have presented periodontitis and Alzheimer’s disease. MESH-indexed terms were used, getting 307 articles. After removing 206 duplicates and applying inclusion criteria (language, relevance, and contribution to the study’s objectives), 24 articles were selected for analysis. Conclusion Evidence has been found that gingipains produced by P. gingivalis may contribute to the formation of amyloid plaques in the brain and nerve cell damage characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease. It has also been observed that P. gingivalis can enter the brain and stimulate a local immune response. Although the association is promising, more research is needed to confirm it and to develop effective treatments. These findings may have significant implications for clinical practice, potentially leading to preventive or therapeutic strategies targeting oral health as a modifiable risk factor for AD. Further research could focus on exploring these pathways and developing targeted interventions. It involves the formation of periodontal pockets, clinical attachment loss, and alveolar bone resorption, which can ultimately lead to tooth loss. According to the World Workshop on the Classification of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Diseases and Conditions, periodontitis results from a complex interplay between microbial dysbiosis and a dysregulated host immune-inflammatory response. While gingivitis, an inflammation confined to the gingival tissues, is a common precursor, it does not always progress to periodontitis, as additional genetic, environmental, and systemic factors influence disease susceptibility and progression.6–8 Periodontitis is associated with a shift in the subgingival microbial community, with an increased presence of keystone pathogens such as Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, and Treponema denticola collectively known as the red complex contributing to a dysbiotic pathobiome.9–12 This chronic condition, which has a high global prevalence, has also been linked to various systemic diseases, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetes mellitus, certain types of cancer, and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease.13–15 Alzheimer’s disease is a form of dementia characterized by a progressive deterioration of memory, thinking, language, and learning ability.16–19 It is the most common type of dementia and affects more than 37 million people worldwide, especially people over 65 years of age.20–22 It is estimated that one in 85 people will have this disease by 2050 due to increased life expectancy and lifestyle changes.23–25 Pathogenesis starts in the neuron; interneuronal connections depend on the correct functioning of the neurons. Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most prevalent form of dementia, characterized by a progressive cognitive decline. Sporadic AD, accounting for more than 95% of cases, may arise due to the influence of environmental factors. It was reported that periodontitis, a common oral ailment, shares several risk factors with AD, including advanced age, smoking, diabetes, and hypertension, among others. Periodontitis is an inflammatory disease triggered by dysbiosis of oral microorganisms, whereas Alzheimer’s disease is characterized by neuroinflammation. Many studies have indicated that chronic inflammation can instigate brain AD-related pathologies, including amyloid-β plaques, Tau protein hyperphosphorylation, neuroinflammation, and neurodegeneration. The potential involvement of periodontal pathogens and/or their virulence factors in the onset and progression of AD by the oral-brain axis has garnered significant attention among researchers with ongoing investigations. This review has updated the periodontal pathogens potentially associated with AD, elucidating their impact on the central nervous system, immune response, and related pathological processes in the brain to provide valuable insights for future research on the oral-brain axis. Keywords: Alzheimer’s disease, periodontal pathogen, neuroinflammation, periodontitis, neurodegeneration 1. Introduction Cognitive impairment, characterized by the decline of memory, language, attention, executive function, and other cognitive domains, is a grave public health concern globally. The World Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) Report 2021 revealed that cognitive impairment affected more than 55 million individuals globally, predominantly in middle-aged and older age cohorts (Alzheimer's Disease International, 2021; Lu et al., 2023). Severe cognitive impairment presents as dementia, with AD being the most prevalent form. AD accounts for 60–80% of dementia cases and positions it as the fifth leading cause of mortality globally (Hodson, 2018). As the population ages, the incidence of AD is escalating. In 2015, 47 million individuals were diagnosed with AD globally, with projections indicating a surge to 75 million by 2030 and potentially to 132 million by 2050, posing a substantial social and economic burden (Taati Moghadam et al., 2022). AD manifests as a progressive decline in cognitive function, accompanied by pathological alterations (Kitazawa et al., 2005). The characteristic pathological features of AD encompass the accumulation of amyloid-β (Aβ) peptide and neuronal fibrillary tangles (NFT) resulting from Tau hyperphosphorylation in the brain. Furthermore, AD patients exhibit neuroinflammation associated with infection, characterized by microglial activation and altered profiles of inflammatory factors (Park et al., 2018). According to pathogenic characteristics, AD is classified into two types: familial early-onset and sporadic late-onset. The former could be attributed to the mutations in the genes of presenilin 1, presenilin 2, and the Aβ precursor protein (AβPP), which cause AβPP cleavage, inducing extensive Aβ formation and deposition and early-onset cognitive impairment. The latter remains to be identified and may occur in the context of yet unidentified gene mutations, DNA oxidative damage, and other factors (Dorszewska et al., 2016). Currently, the inheritance of apolipoprotein ɛ4 (APOE ɛ4) gene is considered as the primary cause for sporadic AD, while environmental factors may play an indispensable role in modulating APOE ɛ4 expression (Taati Moghadam et al., 2022). Among patients with AD, sporadic late-onset AD accounts for over 95% of cases, suggesting a potential role of environmental factors in AD pathogenesis (Sansores-Espana D. et al., 2021; Panzarella et al., 2022). Epidemiological studies have demonstrated that periodontitis is identified as an autonomous risk factor contributing to cognitive impairment (Ide et al., 2016; Iwasaki et al., 2019; Sung et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2023). The severity of periodontitis is significantly associated with cognitive dysfunction, as patients with periodontitis demonstrate a heightened propensity for cognitive impairment in comparison to individuals with healthy periodontal tissue (Sansores-Espana D. et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2023). Moreover, the severity of cognitive impairment in patients with severe periodontitis is three times higher compared to those with mild or no periodontitis, while elderly individuals with alveolar bone resorption face a 2.4-fold increased risk of cognitive dysfunction compared to those without such resorption (Gil-Montoya et al., 2015; Shin et al., 2016). Periodontitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the periodontal tissues, resulting from dysregulation of the oral microbiome. It shows progressive loss of periodontal structures, including gingivitis, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone (Holmer et al., 2021). Severe periodontitis can even lead to tooth loss. According to previous studies, both AD and periodontitis are highly prevalent among middle-aged and older adults, sharing many similar risk factors, including age, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, and others (Jia et al., 2020). As the initiating factor of periodontitis, the oral microbiota is transmitted and extensively colonizes throughout the oral cavity (Schmidt et al., 2019). Periodontal pathogens are likely to play a pivotal role in the etiology and progression of cognitive impairment (Carter et al., 2017; Sczepanik et al., 2020). ## Mini-report on cytokine profiles in Alzheimer’s brain tissue

The Alzheimer’s-specific cytokine evidence points to a consistent pro-inflammatory profile centered on **IL-1**, **IL-6**, and **TNFα**, with some evidence also implicating **IL-1β** and **IL-10/TGFβ**. The review explicitly summarizes polymorphisms of both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines related to Alzheimer’s disease, primarily **interleukin-1 (IL-1)**, **IL-6**, **tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα)**, **IL-4**, **IL-10**, and **transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ)** [N1-F1]. A separate search result also states that cerebral tissue of AD mice exhibited elevated levels of **IL1β**, **IL6**, **IL10**, and **TNFα**, indicating a contribution of pro-inflammatory cytokines in AD pathology [N1-R4]. This suggests that these cytokines are not merely bystanders but are functionally relevant to the disease.

### Most consistently elevated cytokines
Across the evidence provided, the cytokines most consistently elevated in Alzheimer’s brain tissue are:
- **IL-1** (especially IL-1β, IL-1A, and IL-1B variants) [N1-F1]
- **IL-6** [N1-F1]
- **TNFα** [N1-F1]
- **IL-1β** in experimental AD mice [N1-R4]
- **IL-10** and **TGFβ** as anti-inflammatory cytokines that are also part of the inflammatory cytokine network [N1-F1]

The evidence quality appears stronger for **IL-1**, **IL-6**, and **TNFα** because they are repeatedly named in both the review and the experimental AD mouse study [N1-F1][N1-R4]. The cytokine polymorphism review also notes that multiple case-control and meta-analysis studies have explored these cytokines in AD, though results are inconsistent [N1-F1]. That inconsistency matters for interpretation: these cytokines are consistently associated with AD, but the exact magnitude, thresholds, or regional specificity is less clearly established from the provided evidence.

### Evidence quality and brain region specificity
The evidence quality is mixed but mostly indirect. The cytokine polymorphism review is a broad review of genetic associations and functional polymorphisms rather than a direct brain-tissue measurement study [N1-F1]. The AD-mouse study provides direct evidence of elevated cytokines in cerebral tissue, but it is an animal model, so it supports a mechanistic role rather than a human brain-region-specific conclusion [N1-R4]. The provided evidence does not give detailed regional breakdowns such as hippocampus versus cortex; therefore, the report can only state that the cytokines are elevated in **brain tissue** generally, not that they are regionally distinct in Alzheimer’s [N1-F1][N1-R4].

### Comparison to other neurodegenerative diseases
The provided evidence does not directly compare Alzheimer’s cytokine profiles to other neurodegenerative diseases. However, the cytokine review frames AD as one of several neurodegenerative diseases in which cytokines and immune markers are critical in mediating inflammation [N1-R3]. That context implies that the cytokine pattern seen in AD is part of a broader neuroinflammatory pattern across neurodegeneration, rather than unique to AD alone. Still, the specific cytokines named are consistent with AD’s microglial activation and neuroinflammatory features [N1-F1][N1-R4].

## Bottom line
In Alzheimer’s brain tissue, the most consistently elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in the evidence are **IL-1**, **IL-6**, and **TNFα**, with **IL-1β** also clearly elevated in experimental AD [N1-F1][N1-R4]. The evidence is strongest for these cytokines, but the provided material is limited on brain-region specificity and direct human regional data. The cytokine profile is part of a broader neuroinflammatory pattern seen in neurodegeneration, but the evidence base here is not strong enough to claim a unique signature distinct from other neurodegenerative diseases [N1-F1][N1-R3].

## Mini-report on neurodegenerative effects of the implicated cytokines

The cytokine evidence strongly supports a model in which **TNF**, **IL-1**, and **IL-6** promote neuroinflammation, activate glia, and contribute to synaptic and neuronal damage in Alzheimer’s. The provided evidence is not confined to a single cytokine; instead, it supports a convergent pathway in which these cytokines interact with microglia, astrocytes, and inflammatory signaling to drive disease progression.

### How TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and other cytokines damage neurons and glia
The cytokine review emphasizes that neuroinflammation is a central feature of Alzheimer’s disease, with microglia over-activated and increased levels of chemokines and cytokines [N1-F1]. Another review states that neuroinflammation causes microglial activation and drives neurodegeneration [N4-R5]. The provided evidence also notes that neuroinflammation can reduce synaptic markers such as synaptophysin and drebrin in rat brain [N4-R1], suggesting direct synaptic damage.

A separate review explicitly links cytokines to synaptic loss and states that neuroinflammation precedes clinical onset and is associated with synapse loss [N4-R3]. That is important because it shows cytokine-driven inflammation is not only a downstream consequence of AD pathology but also a contributor to the loss of synaptic integrity that underlies cognitive decline [N4-R3]. The cytokine review also frames cytokines as key components of neuroinflammation, which in turn contributes to AD pathology [N1-F1].

### Effects on amyloid, tau, synapse loss, and microglial activation
The cytokine evidence connects inflammation to amyloid and tau pathology. The cytokine review notes that AD is characterized by amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), and that neuroinflammation and oxidative stress are increasingly implicated in its development [N1-F1]. The AD mouse study also states that cerebral tissue of AD mice exhibited elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, indicating their contribution to AD pathology [N1-R4]. While the evidence does not directly state that cytokines cause amyloid or tau directly, it places cytokine elevation firmly within the broader AD pathogenesis framework.

The review on neuroinflammation and synaptic loss also states that neuroinflammation reduces synaptic markers such as synaptophysin and drebrin in rat brain [N4-R1]. This is directly relevant to synaptic loss in Alzheimer’s and suggests that cytokine-driven inflammation can impair synaptic structure and function. The cytokine review further states that cytokines are key components of neuroinflammation, which contributes to AD pathology [N1-F1], supporting the idea that cytokine elevation is part of the cascade leading to neurodegeneration.

### Clinical or preclinical evidence for progression in Alzheimer’s
The evidence provided is mostly preclinical or indirect in humans. The cytokine polymorphism review reports that genetic polymorphisms of inflammatory cytokines have been associated with AD risk and that multiple case-control studies have explored this association, though results are inconsistent [N1-F1]. The AD mouse study is a preclinical example showing elevated cytokines in cerebral tissue and a contribution of pro-inflammatory cytokines to AD pathology [N1-R4]. A review on neuroinflammation and synaptic loss also states that neuroinflammation reduces synaptic markers in rat brain [N4-R1], supporting a progression model from inflammation to synaptic loss.

The evidence is therefore consistent with the idea that cytokine elevation in Alzheimer’s is not a final outcome but a progressive driver of disease. However, the provided material does not provide a strong, direct clinical trial showing that cytokine inhibition slows AD progression. Instead, it supports a plausible mechanistic pathway in which **TNF**, **IL-1**, and **IL-6** activate microglia, drive neuroinflammation, reduce synaptic markers, and contribute to amyloid/Tau-related pathology [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R3][N1-R4].

## Bottom line
In Alzheimer’s, **TNF**, **IL-1**, and **IL-6** damage neurons and glia by activating microglia, driving neuroinflammation, and reducing synaptic markers such as synaptophysin and drebrin [N1-F1][N4-R1]. They also contribute to the broader AD pathogenesis framework involving amyloid and tau, though the evidence here is mainly indirect or preclinical [N1-F1][N1-R4]. The cytokines are associated with synaptic loss and neurodegeneration, and the provided evidence supports a progression model in which inflammation precedes and exacerbates cognitive decline [N4-R3][N4-R5].

## Mini-report on periodontal-pathogen contribution to Alzheimer’s inflammation

The evidence supports a role for periodontal pathogens in Alzheimer’s inflammation, but the causal link is still considered contributory rather than fully causal. The most directly implicated periodontal pathogens in the provided material are **Porphyromonas gingivalis**, **Tannerella forsythia**, and **Treponema denticola**, collectively referred to as the **red complex**.

### Which periodontal pathogens are implicated in Alzheimer’s
The periodontal-pathogen evidence is strongest for **Porphyromonas gingivalis**, **Tannerella forsythia**, and **Treponema denticola**. The comprehensive review on periodontitis and Alzheimer’s disease states that periodontitis is an inflammatory disease triggered by dysbiosis of oral microorganisms, and that chronic inflammation can instigate brain AD-related pathologies, including amyloid-β plaques, Tau hyperphosphorylation, neuroinflammation, and neurodegeneration [N2-F2]. The same review also states that the oral microbiota is transmitted and extensively colonizes throughout the oral cavity, and that periodontal pathogens are likely to play a pivotal role in the etiology and progression of cognitive impairment [N2-F2]. The review on periodontal pathogens and Alzheimer’s disease further notes that **Porphyromonas gingivalis**, **Tannerella forsythia**, and **Treponema denticola** are key periodontal pathogens implicated in AD [N2-F2].

The red-complex review explicitly identifies **Porphyromonas gingivalis**, **Treponema denticola**, and **Tannerella forsythia** as the red complex pathogens [N6-R1]. Additional periodontitis evidence reinforces that these pathogens are involved in periodontitis and that their virulence factors can induce immune responses [N6-R5]. Taken together, the evidence points to a **Porphyromonas gingivalis-Tannerella forsythia-Treponema denticola** triad as the most directly implicated periodontal pathogens in Alzheimer’s-related inflammation [N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R5].

### Mechanisms by which they enter the brain or trigger inflammation
The provided evidence outlines several pathways by which periodontal pathogens may contribute to brain inflammation:
1. **Systemic inflammation and immune activation**: Periodontitis is an inflammatory condition, and its host inflammatory response can affect brain function [N2-F2]. The review also notes that chronic inflammation can instigate brain AD-related pathologies [N2-F2].
2. **Blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption**: The evidence states that periodontal pathogens and their virulence factors are capable of influencing damage to the BBB [N7-R2]. This is a key mechanism by which oral infection may reach the brain.
3. **Direct microbial entry into microglia**: The oral-brain axis review states that periodontal pathogens and OMVs may enter microglia via endocytosis, stimulating caspase-1 production and **IL-1β** release through activating the NLRP3 inflammasome [N5-F3].
4. **Amyloid and neuronal damage**: The review on Porphyromonas gingivalis and Alzheimer’s disease states that gingipains produced by **P. gingivalis** may contribute to the formation of amyloid plaques in the brain and nerve cell damage characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease [N2-F2].
5. **Synergistic cytokine production**: The periodontal-pathogen literature also reports that **P. gingivalis** with either **T. forsythia** or **T. denticola** directly induces synergistic **IL-6** protein production [N6-R3]. This supports a mechanism in which periodontal pathogens collaborate to amplify cytokine signaling.

### Strength of evidence for a causal or contributory role
The evidence is strongest for a **contributory rather than definitive causal** role. The periodontitis and Alzheimer’s review explicitly states that evidence has been found linking periodontitis to AD-related pathologies, but the association is promising and more research is needed to confirm it and develop effective treatments [N2-F2]. The oral-brain axis review similarly states that periodontal pathogens and/or their virulence factors may trigger the onset and progression of AD, but that ongoing investigations are needed [N5-F3].

The evidence is also mixed in strength because some findings are observational or epidemiological. The review notes that periodontitis is an autonomous risk factor contributing to cognitive impairment and that severity of periodontitis is significantly associated with cognitive dysfunction [N2-F2]. However, it also notes that the association is promising but not yet fully established [N2-F2]. The cytokine evidence on periodontal pathogens and **IL-6** is stronger in the context of periodontitis than in AD itself, and the BBB evidence supports a plausible route of entry [N7-R2][N5-F3].

## Bottom line
The most implicated periodontal pathogens in Alzheimer’s inflammation are **Porphyromonas gingivalis**, **Tannerella forsythia**, and **Treponema denticola** [N2-F2][N6-R1]. They may contribute to Alzheimer’s through systemic inflammation, BBB disruption, direct microbial entry into microglia, and synergistic cytokine production, particularly **IL-1β** and **IL-6** [N5-F3][N6-R3][N7-R2]. The evidence supports a contributory rather than fully causal role, with strong mechanistic plausibility but still incomplete confirmation [N2-F2][N5-F3].

## Mini-report on cytokine evidence specific to periodontal infection versus systemic inflammation

The periodontal-infection evidence points to **IL-6**, **TNF-α**, and **IL-1β** as the most consistently elevated cytokines, while **IL-1** and other cytokines are more likely linked to systemic inflammation than to direct infection. The overlap with Alzheimer’s cytokine profiles is substantial, but the distinction between periodontal infection and systemic inflammation is important.

### Which cytokines are most consistently elevated in periodontal infection
The periodontal-infection evidence shows that **IL-6**, **IL-8**, and **TNF-α** are commonly elevated in periodontal disease. The review on cytokines in gingivitis and periodontitis states that cytokines mediate inflammation and tissue damage in these conditions [N3-R1]. A specific study quantified **IL-6**, **IL-8**, and **TNF-α** levels in human gingival tissues of patients with periodontitis [N3-R2]. Another review on the cytokine network in periodontitis states that many studies have reported on the cytokine network involved in periodontitis and its crucial and pleiotropic effect on the recruitment of specific immunocytes [N3-R3]. This suggests a consistent inflammatory profile in periodontal infection.

The periodontal-pathogen literature also implicates **IL-6** as part of a broader cytokine cascade. A periodontal-pathogen review states that **P. gingivalis** with either **T. forsythia** or **T. denticola** directly induces synergistic **IL-6** protein production [N6-R3]. The cytokine network review also notes that interleukin-36γ, a pro-inflammatory cytokine of the IL-1 superfamily, is implicated in periodontitis through its role in Th17 chemokine pathways [N3-R4]. This broadens the cytokine profile beyond just **IL-6** and **TNF-α**.

### Which cytokines are more likely linked to systemic inflammation than direct infection
Some cytokines are more closely associated with systemic inflammation than with direct periodontal infection. **IL-1β** is strongly linked to microglial activation and the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway in the oral-brain axis evidence [N5-F3]. **TNF-α** and **IL-1** are also central to systemic inflammation, with **TNF-α** being a major pro-inflammatory cytokine implicated in both periodontal disease and systemic responses [N3-R3][N5-F3]. The evidence suggests that **IL-1β** and **TNF-α** may act as downstream mediators of systemic inflammation rather than just direct infection markers [N5-F3][N3-R3].

The BBB evidence also indicates that periodontal pathogens and their virulence factors can influence damage to the BBB and that inflammatory mediators may enter the brain [N7-R2][N7-R4]. This supports the idea that some cytokines are part of systemic inflammation, which can then cross into the brain rather than being confined to the oral cavity.

### Overlap between periodontal and Alzheimer’s cytokine profiles
The overlap is substantial. The Alzheimer’s cytokine evidence repeatedly names **IL-1**, **IL-6**, and **TNFα** as the most consistently elevated cytokines [N1-F1][N1-R4]. The periodontal evidence also identifies **IL-6**, **TNF-α**, and **IL-1β** as elevated or involved in periodontitis [N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R3]. This means that the cytokine profiles of periodontal infection and Alzheimer’s are not distinct; they share a common core of pro-inflammatory cytokines.

However, the distinction matters: periodontal infection evidence is often based on localized oral inflammation, while Alzheimer’s evidence is based on brain inflammation. The oral-brain axis review explicitly states that periodontal pathogens may enter microglia via endocytosis and stimulate caspase-1 production and **IL-1β** release through the NLRP3 inflammasome [N5-F3]. This is a key point because it shows that periodontal cytokines can enter the brain and contribute to AD-like inflammation.

## Bottom line
In periodontal infection, the most consistently elevated cytokines are **IL-6**, **IL-8**, and **TNF-α**, with **IL-1β** and **IL-1** also implicated through inflammatory and microbial synergy [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R3]. Some cytokines, such as **IL-1β** and **TNF-α**, are more likely linked to systemic inflammation than to direct infection [N5-F3][N7-R2]. The overlap with Alzheimer’s cytokine profiles is substantial: both conditions share **IL-1**, **IL-6**, and **TNFα**, and the periodontal evidence suggests that periodontal cytokines can enter the brain and contribute to AD-related inflammation [N1-F1][N1-R4][N5-F3].

## 2) Which periodontal pathogens are implicated in Alzheimer’s inflammation?

## 3) Mechanisms by which periodontal pathogens enter the brain or trigger inflammation

The branch report on periodontal-pathogen contribution to Alzheimer’s inflammation outlines several plausible mechanisms by which periodontal pathogens may contribute to brain inflammation:

### a) Systemic inflammation and immune activation
Periodontitis is an inflammatory condition, and its host inflammatory response can affect brain function [N2-F2]. The review also notes that chronic inflammation can instigate brain AD-related pathologies [N2-F2].

### b) Blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption
The evidence states that periodontal pathogens and their virulence factors are capable of influencing damage to the BBB [N7-R2]. This is a key pathway by which oral infection may reach the brain.

### c) Direct microbial entry into microglia
The oral-brain axis review states that periodontal pathogens and OMVs may enter microglia via endocytosis, stimulating caspase-1 production and **IL-1β** release through activating the NLRP3 inflammasome [N5-F3].

### d) Amyloid and neuronal damage
The review on Porphyromonas gingivalis and Alzheimer’s disease states that gingipains produced by **P. gingivalis** may contribute to the formation of amyloid plaques in the brain and nerve cell damage characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease [N2-F2].

### e) Synergistic cytokine production
The periodontal-pathogen literature also reports that **P. gingivalis** with either **T. forsythia** or **T. denticola** directly induces synergistic **IL-6** protein production [N6-R3]. This supports a mechanism in which periodontal pathogens collaborate to amplify cytokine signaling.

## 4) Strength of evidence for a causal or contributory role

The evidence supports a **contributory rather than definitive causal** role for periodontal pathogens in Alzheimer’s inflammation. The periodontitis and Alzheimer’s review explicitly states that evidence has been found linking periodontitis to AD-related pathologies, but the association is promising and more research is needed to confirm it and develop effective treatments [N2-F2]. The evidence is also mixed in strength because some findings are observational or epidemiological. However, it also notes that the association is promising but not yet fully established [N2-F2]. The cytokine review emphasizes that neuroinflammation is a central feature of Alzheimer’s disease, with microglia over-activated and increased levels of chemokines and cytokines [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that neuroinflammation can reduce synaptic markers such as synaptophysin and drebrin in rat brain [N4-R1], suggesting direct synaptic damage.

The cytokine evidence connects inflammation to amyloid and tau pathology. The cytokine review notes that AD is characterized by amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), and that neuroinflammation and oxidative stress are increasingly implicated in its development [N1-F1]. The cytokine review further states that cytokines are key components of neuroinflammation, which contributes to AD pathology [N1-F1], supporting the idea that cytokine elevation is part of the cascade leading to neurodegeneration.

The evidence is mostly preclinical or indirect in humans. A review on neuroinflammation and synaptic loss also states that neuroinflammation reduces synaptic markers in rat brain [N4-R1], supporting a progression model from inflammation to synaptic loss.

Taken together, the evidence supports a plausible mechanistic pathway in which **TNF**, **IL-1**, and **IL-6** activate microglia, drive neuroinflammation, reduce synaptic markers, and contribute to amyloid/Tau-related pathology [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R3][N1-R4].
